label: Krishnan, 78, at home in Chennai
blurb: Six months after a stroke. Severe expressive aphasia; his daughter Priya calls from Bengaluru and Meera comes in by day.
speaker_note: A retired civil engineer. He understands everything said to him and gets very few words out, usually one or two. Meera is the carer who comes on weekday mornings; his daughter Priya lives in Bengaluru and calls in the evening. He tires quickly and asks for help rather than announcing plans.

label: Anya Sharma, 32, three months after a hemorrhagic stroke
blurb: Marketing professional living with her parents. Understands everything, loses the words, and hates having to be helped.
speaker_note: Anya is thirty-two, three months after a hemorrhagic stroke, living in her parents' flat in Mumbai with her mother almost always in the room. Her comprehension is intact and her expressive aphasia is severe: she gets one or two content words out, often repeating the first sound, and abandons the sentence rather than fight it. She is young, informal and increasingly blunt, so her messages should be short and direct rather than polite - 'Not now, Ma.', 'I am tired.', 'Give me my phone.' Most of what she says is practical: the toilet, water, her right hand hurting, the splint, physio, and her phone, which she asks for many times a day. On foggy or exhausted days she asks for less and refuses more, and losing her independence is what she resents most, so never soften a refusal into an apology.

label: Captain Vikram Singh, 38, rehabilitation ward near Pune
blurb: Seven months after a head injury on operations, he finds his words slowly and speaks to the staff around him, not to family.
speaker_note: Captain Vikram Singh is thirty-eight, seven months after a severe traumatic brain injury sustained on operations that caused a stroke-like event, living on a ward at a military rehabilitation centre near Pune. His left side is weak and he needs an orderly, a nurse or his physiotherapist to move him at all; his wife Rina and son Rohan are far away in Rajasthan and reach him only on scheduled video calls, so almost everyone he speaks to is staff. He does not have aphasia and his grammar is intact, but words go missing under fatigue and pressure and he loses the thread of what he was assembling, so an utterance arrives as two or three content words after a long pause. He states things rather than pleading, and is more formal and more specific about time and place than most speakers: clipped, close to a report. He hates asking for help with basics and asks anyway, without softening it.

label: Grace Okonkwo, 61, alone in a council flat with a changing care rota
blurb: Two years after a stroke, living alone in Manchester with agency carers who change week to week and a daughter in London.
speaker_note: Grace Okonkwo is 61, born in Nigeria and in England since she was 24, and she speaks Igbo and English with a Nigerian accent the recognizer handles poorly. A stroke two years ago took most of her speech; she manages one or two content words at a time and tires by the end of a sentence. She lives alone, so there is often nobody in the room: many of her messages are aimed at whoever has just come through the door, or are about the buzzer, the phone, the post, or something she cannot reach from her chair. Her care comes from a rotating agency rota, mainly Donna and Dawn, whose names she cannot always make the machine hear apart, plus her neighbour Eunice, her church, and her daughter Ngozi who rings on Sundays. She is independent-minded and slightly formal, learned English carefully and still speaks it that way, and she asks for things plainly with please rather than softening them.

label: Bea Halloran, 84, a small care home in rural Ireland
blurb: One or two words at a time, four years after a stroke; almost all of the meaning has to come from what is known about her.
speaker_note: Bea is eighty-four and has lived in a small rural care home since her stroke four years ago. The people around her are the care assistants on shift, most often Nuala, and her daughter Kathleen, who visits at the weekend. She manages one or two words at a time, tires within minutes of trying, and is hard of hearing, so she rarely repeats herself once she has been understood. Her comprehension is intact but slow: she follows what is said to her and will nod or shake her head, given time. Keep her words to the fewest that carry the need, and never make her more fluent than she is.

label: Tomás, 45, working part-time in Lisbon
blurb: Fourteen months after a brainstem stroke. Mild dysarthria only: his words are all there, but strangers and phone lines lose them.
speaker_note: A Brazilian-born operations analyst living in Lisbon, working part-time and remotely in English, his third language. A brainstem stroke fourteen months ago left him with mild dysarthria: his speech is slurred and effortful and tires within a few sentences, but his language, vocabulary and judgement are completely intact. He is usually alone at his desk or out in the city, so most of what he says goes to a colleague, a waiter, a taxi driver or a receptionist rather than a carer; his partner Inês is with him at home in the evening. He says whole adult sentences and does not want them shortened for him, and his commonest frustrations are being asked to repeat himself, phone calls, and noisy rooms.
